question:
Τοπωνύμια πειρατικών και κουρσάρικων ορμητηρίων στην Ανατολική Μεσόγειο (1600-1700)
Research scope: Νέα πραγματική αναζήτηση για τοπωνύμια ορμητηρίων, αγκυροβολίων και καταφυγίων κουρσάρων στην Ανατολική Μεσόγειο τον 17ο αιώνα. Έλεγξε περιηγητές, portolans, σύγχρονα κείμενα, αρχεία και μεταγενέστερες μελέτες. Για κάθε εύρημα δώσε ιστορικό όνομα, τεκμηριωμένη σύγχρονη ταύτιση και συντεταγμένες όπου υπάρχουν, χρονολογία γεγονότος, χρήστες, χρήση, ακριβή πηγή/σελίδα/φύλλο/αρχειακή αναφορά και απόσπασμα. Άγνωστα στοιχεία μένουν άγνωστα. Διαχώρισε τεκμήριο, ερμηνεία, υπόθεση και ανεξάρτητη διασταύρωση.

of Chios. However, Aegean folk legends may have preserved aspects of his activities that historical accounts
have overlooked. Manetas is etched into the popular consciousness due to his tumultuous personal life. Legend
has it that he married the beautiful Marioga in Melos, leaving her under the care of the island’s bishop when
he embarked on a pirate expedition. Marioga, steadfastly refusing the bishop’s advances, was falsely accused of
infidelity to Manetas. Subsequently, Manetas captured her and executed her at his place of business. This tragic
episode forms the central theme of “Manetas’ rhyme”, a popular Aegean folk song known in various renditions
today (Legrand 1874, 296–300; Spyridakis and Petropoulos 1962, 375–78; Poulianos 1964, 121–24). While each
version features adaptations of hero names and locales, the Ikarian rendition places Manetas’s attempt “in the
straits of Samos” (stes Samos ta boghazia), with his wife’s murder purportedly occurring there. Accordingly,
local traditions suggest that the murder took place either in Ikaria or Phournoi, specifically in the bays of Pano
and Kato Maneta. Nonetheless, whether Stathis Romanos Manetas utilized Phournoi as a base and secure anchorage during his operations in the Chios area in 1694 and 1695 remains a conjecture. Offspring of Manetas
continued the family tradition, engaging in acts of piracy for the most part of the first half of the 18th century
(Krantonelli 1998, 35–8, 168–69).

evidence.text:
History generally records Lord Cornwallis's surrender at Yorktown in October 1781 as the last battle of the American Revolution. Nevertheless, six months after that epic campaign, warships of the South Carolina Navy commanded by Commodore Alexander Gillon, transported Spanish General Juan Manuel de Cagigal's infantrymen from Havana to Nassau in the Bahamas, where the British capitulated on May 8, 1782. Thus, the Treaty of Versailles signed the following year made this little-known Spanish and American expedition the last battle of the American Revolution.
The Bahamas, or Lucayos, an archipelago off the southeastern coast of the United States, take on increasing historical interest with the approach of the 500th Anniversary of Columbus's first landing in the New World 200 miles southeast of Nassau at Guanahani. The Bahamas, however, played only a minor role in the Spanish colonization of the Americas whereas, Great Britain gave priority to these strategic islands, making an initial settlement on the island of Eleuthera. The British later found a better harbor to the west and named the island New Providence which became their Bahama stronghold. King Charles II granted the Duke of Albemarle the Bahamas in 1670 and appointed John Wentworth as governor. Harrassed by plundering pirates, the British governor constructed a fort on New Providence in 1695 and named it Nassau in honor of King William III. The island's preoccupation changed in 1703 from marauding corsairs to a Spanish and French invasion during the War of the Spanish Succession. Great Britain regained control and maintained it until the outbreak of the American Revolution when John Paul Jones participated in the brief American seizure of Nassau in March 1776 in one of the first offensive operations in the history of the United States Navy.
